groundTruthNarrative: Arts' 9-day median resolution is mostly a routing effect, not general neglect. Since 2025-08-18, rule RR-17 has sent every SlotBook ticket to a 0.4-FTE best-effort queue, where tickets wait a median 17 days before anyone touches them. Removing these tickets closes 70% of the gap. Matched by category and priority, Arts non-SlotBook tickets are handled like everyone else's. The remaining gap comes from the on-site hardware mix at the Lindqvist campus, where a technician is on site only two days a week; Education, on the same campus, shows the same delay. The Dean's general-neglect story is wrong. The ITS Director's story is also overstated: volume is 2.7x, not 3x, and 1.6x remains without SlotBook, with no excess of trivial or duplicate tickets. Requesters were never told about the best-effort track, because the P4 acknowledgement is silent. Whether Arts leadership was told in August 2025 cannot be established: there is no document, and the only other witness declined to be interviewed. Whether the SSO migration caused the SlotBook surge is confounded by term start and by the new ticket category. Neither open question blocks a forward fix: an explicit support decision for SlotBook and honest requester messaging.

answers.rationale: H1 claims Arts is slowed because it is Arts. In the category- and priority-matched comparison (E4), Arts non-SlotBook tickets are within 0.3 days of non-Arts tickets in every sizeable remotely handled category. The one slower category, on-site hardware, is equally slow for Education on the same campus (E5: 6.5 vs 6.4 days), so it is location-driven, not faculty-driven. The History administrator reports fast normal service (E10). The lecturer's three-week 'proof' (E11) was mostly time awaiting the requester, with first response in 0.4 days (E12). The survey (E13) locates dissatisfaction mainly in SlotBook. The evidence counts against faculty-level deprioritisation.

E3 gives the 9.0 vs 3.0 medians. E4 shows that all 1,610 SlotBook tickets went to P4 with a 21-day median, and that excluding them drops Arts to 4.8 days, closing 4.2 of the 6.0-day gap (70%, i.e. most). E6 documents the routing rule, and E16 shows P4 is staffed at 0.4 FTE. No rival explains that 70%.

The ITS Director claims 3x, 'almost all SlotBook' (E2). The system extract gives 2.7x (E3), and without SlotBook Arts still raises 1.92 tickets per account, 1.6x the university average (E4). SlotBook is a large contributor but does not fully explain the excess, so the 'fully explained' claim is contradicted. E5 shows part of the residual is a heavier on-site hardware load.

This is the irreducible dispute. The Director asserts a verbal briefing of the then Operations Manager on 2025-08-12 (E2); H4 counts a briefing of either the Dean or the Operations Manager. The Dean denies any knowledge (E1), but she was not at the meeting, so her denial does not settle what the manager was told. E8 confirms the meeting happened but finds no agenda, notes or emails, and the only other witness declined to be interviewed. E6's internal-only distribution list shows no written notice, but does not exclude a verbal briefing. E9's manager arrived later and cannot speak to it. The evidence does not discriminate either way.

E7 shows the ACK-P4 template sent for every SlotBook ticket mentions no priority or timeframe, unlike P2 and P3, and was unchanged throughout the period. E10 corroborates that the requester received only the generic 'received' email. This holds regardless of the disputed leadership briefing in H4.

E4 shows Arts' duplicate rate (4.1%) is essentially the university's (3.9%), and Arts' how-to/training share (9%) is lower than non-Arts (11%). The volume excess is in SlotBook and on-site hardware (E4, E5), not trivial or duplicate tickets. The ITS Director's claim in E2 is contradicted.

Temporal order: RR-17 took effect on 2025-08-18, before the academic year measured (E6). Mechanism: P4 has no target and 0.4 FTE (E6, E16). Covariation: P4 tickets median 21 days against 4.8 for other Arts tickets (E4). The main rival, that SlotBook tickets are simply hard, is ruled out: median hands-on time is 1.6 days and median wait before first action is 17 days, so the delay is queueing (E4). The other rival, faculty-wide bias, is ruled out by the matched comparison (E4).

Mechanism: a technician is on site only Tuesday and Thursday, and Lindqvist on-site tickets wait a median 4.7 days for technician arrival versus 0.6 on the main campus, with repair itself under half a day at both (E5). Covariation: on-site hardware median 6.5 days at Lindqvist versus 1.8 on the main campus, and Arts has 31% versus 14% on-site hardware tickets (E5); excluding on-site hardware, Arts non-SlotBook median is 3.1 days, essentially the university's 3.0 (E4). Rival ruled out: Education on the same campus shows the same 6.4-day on-site median, and Arts is at parity within matched remote categories (E4), so the residual reflects the coverage schedule acting on Arts' on-site-heavy mix, not Arts-specific treatment.

The SlotBook ticket rise coincides with the SSO go-live (E14), and an administrator attributes the login problems to it (E10). But three things confound the link. The category was created only on 2025-08-18, and earlier keyword counts undercount, so the level rise may be a measurement artifact. September is the annual timetabling peak: the September 2025 spike (241 vs 134 average, about 1.8x) is in line with the September 2024 keyword ratio (58 vs about 31 a month, about 1.9x), so seasonality alone could explain the spike without refuting an SSO effect. ITS states SlotBook was not SSO-integrated but has no logs to prove it (E15). Co-occurrence is established; causation is neither established nor contradicted.

The antecedent, that neither the Dean nor the Operations Manager was told, is itself unestablished (see I4, E8): the Dean was very likely not told directly, but whether the Operations Manager was cannot be determined. With no known state of the antecedent, the evidence cannot show even an association between it and the Dean's perception, nor count against one. The Dean's view is in any case also fed by real SlotBook delays (E1, E4).

Arts' non-SlotBook tickets (2,260 a year) are currently served at parity (E4, E10). Moving them into a 0.4-FTE queue with no target (E16) would extend multi-week delays to laptops, email and teaching-room hardware for 1,180 staff. That punishes all Arts users for one application and worsens outcomes.

It targets the established mechanism: an unowned application routed to a target-less queue (E4, E6, E17). It also targets the established communication failure at the requester level (E7, E10), and it is low-cost and reversible. It does not depend on resolving who said what in August 2025 (E8), because it makes the support status explicit from now on.

Retiring SlotBook could be right if CampusBook meets Arts' timetabling needs. But ITS asserts that it does (E2), Arts says it lacks repeating multi-section patterns (E10), and no fit assessment or migration plan exists (E17). Forcing 1,900 teaching sections onto it within two months commits to an unconfirmed premise.

A split, matched report corrects the misleading headline comparison (E3 vs E4) that drives both leaders' narratives, so it is reasonable. It is monitoring only, however: it does not change the routing or support status that causes the gap, so it is not among the best next actions.

The proposed Arts desk would take over all Arts tickets: 3,870 a year (E3) for 2 FTE, about 1,935 per FTE, against about 565 per FTE (11,860 / 21) on a central desk already at 94% utilisation (E16). The new desk would be several times overloaded, so Arts' non-SlotBook service, currently at parity (E4), would deteriorate. The residual gap is a campus on-site schedule shared with Education that an Arts desk does not change (E5), and SlotBook has no documentation or support agreement for two new staff to work from (E17). The proposal rests on the contradicted H1 and is likely to worsen outcomes for Arts staff.

The mechanism behind most of the gap is established (E4, E6, E16), and so is the requester-level communication failure (E7). That is enough to commit to the substantive support-status and messaging intervention (A2). The open questions do not change it: the August 2025 dispute (E8) is about history and cannot be resolved from records, and the SSO/surge question (E14) bears only on SlotBook's future.
